prompt: Which method of authorizing access to a storage account is the most secure?
choices: Microsoft Entra ID with Azure RBAC data roles
The account's shared access keys, held in a vault
A shared access signature (SAS) token
Anonymous public read access on the container
correctAnswers: Microsoft Entra ID with Azure RBAC data roles
explanation: Entra ID with Azure RBAC data roles is identity-based, so there is no key to leak, rotate or hand over. A SAS is the tempting runner-up because it is scoped and time-limited, however it is still a bearer token: whoever holds it is the caller, and nothing ties it to a person.

prompt: What is a shared access signature (SAS)?
choices: A scoped, time-limited, revocable token
A permanent account-level password for the account
A certificate used only for TLS termination
A managed identity for the storage account
correctAnswers: A scoped, time-limited, revocable token
explanation: A SAS is a scoped, time-limited token granting specific rights, issued without sharing the account key. It is not a password, which is the mental model to avoid — a SAS cannot be changed after issue, so revoking one means either a stored access policy or rotating the signing key.

prompt: Rank the storage authorization methods from most to least secure.
choices: Entra ID + RBAC > user-delegation SAS > account-key SAS > shared key
Shared account key > account-key SAS > user-delegation SAS > Entra ID
Account-key SAS > Entra ID + RBAC > shared key > user-delegation SAS
All four options are equally secure in practice
correctAnswers: Entra ID + RBAC > user-delegation SAS > account-key SAS > shared key
explanation: Identity-based access is strongest, then a user-delegation SAS signed with Entra credentials, then an account-key SAS, with the bare shared key weakest. The ranking follows one question rather than feature count: what has to be shared, and can it be revoked without breaking everything else.

prompt: You must give a partner time-limited read access to a single blob without sharing the account keys. What should you issue?
choices: A user-delegation SAS scoped to that blob
A Reader RBAC role at the subscription scope
The primary account access key, shared
A managed identity for the partner
correctAnswers: A user-delegation SAS scoped to that blob
explanation: A user-delegation SAS scoped to the single blob gives time-bound read access without exposing the account key, and it can be revoked through Entra. A subscription-level Reader role is the tempting answer because it sounds narrow, however it is a control-plane role and grants no data access at all.

prompt: What is the strongest way to prevent shared-key access to a storage account entirely?
choices: Disable shared-key authorization on the account
Set a read-only resource lock on the storage account
Store the account keys in Azure Key Vault
Rotate both account keys every week
correctAnswers: Disable shared-key authorization on the account
explanation: Disabling shared-key access forces all requests through Microsoft Entra authorization. Rotation and vaulting reduce but don't eliminate key use.

prompt: Which identity sources can be used for Azure Files identity-based authentication over SMB?
choices: On-premises AD DS, Entra DS, or Entra Kerberos
Only local user accounts created on each client machine
Only an on-premises AD DS domain, and nothing else
Only Entra application registrations for the share
correctAnswers: On-premises AD DS, Entra DS, or Entra Kerberos
explanation: Azure Files supports on-premises AD DS, Entra Domain Services, and Entra Kerberos for SMB authentication. Answering “only on-premises AD DS” is the dated reading, and it is what pushes teams into deploying a domain controller they cannot justify any more.

prompt: How many identity sources for Azure Files identity-based authentication can be enabled on ONE storage account?
choices: Exactly one at a time
Two — one for SMB, one for NFS
Unlimited, mixed per share
Zero — it is not supported
correctAnswers: Exactly one at a time
explanation: Only one identity source can be enabled per storage account; you can't mix AD DS and Entra Kerberos on the same account.

prompt: After share-level access is granted on an Azure Files share, what provides fine-grained control over individual files and folders?
choices: Windows ACLs, or NTFS permissions
Per-file Azure RBAC data roles on the share
A SAS token issued per file
Blob versioning on the share
correctAnswers: Windows ACLs, or NTFS permissions
explanation: Once share-level access is granted, ordinary Windows NTFS ACLs govern individual files and folders, exactly as on-premises. Per-file Azure RBAC is the tempting answer because RBAC is everywhere else in Azure, but it operates at share level whereas the file-level decision stays with NTFS.

prompt: Which Azure Files identity source requires NO on-premises domain controller?
choices: Microsoft Entra Kerberos
A read-only domain controller
A gMSA on a member server
An on-premises AD DS domain
correctAnswers: Microsoft Entra Kerberos
explanation: Entra Kerberos is the cloud-only identity source, letting Entra users reach shares with no domain controller anywhere. Deploying a read-only domain controller in Azure is the tempting lift-and-shift instinct, however it reintroduces exactly the infrastructure Entra Kerberos removes.

prompt: What does soft delete protect against in Azure Storage?
choices: Accidental or malicious deletion, within a window
Unauthorized read access to the stored data by anyone
Weak TLS versions being negotiated
Slow performance under a heavy load
correctAnswers: Accidental or malicious deletion, within a window
explanation: Soft delete makes deleted blobs, containers and shares recoverable within a retention window, so it defends against accidental and malicious deletion. It is not an access control, which is the confusion worth naming: it changes what you can undo rather than who can read.

prompt: What does blob versioning provide?
choices: A history of previous versions after an overwrite
Access control applied per blob version only, not per blob
Encryption of the blob contents at rest
Automatic geo-replication of the blob
correctAnswers: A history of previous versions after an overwrite
explanation: Versioning preserves the previous state of a blob each time it is overwritten, so you can go back to what it was. It does not encrypt anything, which is the misreading — the protection is against losing content, never against someone reading it.

prompt: What distinguishes immutable storage (WORM) from soft delete and versioning?
choices: It prevents modification or deletion during retention
It only preserves the overwrite history, like versioning
It only recovers deleted data, exactly like soft delete
It is a form of encryption applied at rest
correctAnswers: It prevents modification or deletion during retention
explanation: Secure transfer required forces every request onto HTTPS. Minimum TLS version is the closest miss and a separate setting: it pins which protocol versions are acceptable once HTTPS is already in use, whereas this one is what rejects plaintext HTTP at all.

prompt: A compliance mandate requires that financial records cannot be altered or deleted for 7 years, even by an owner. Which feature meets this?
choices: A time-based immutability (WORM) policy, Locked
A read-only resource lock on the storage account
Soft delete with a seven-year retention window
Blob versioning on the affected container
correctAnswers: A time-based immutability (WORM) policy, Locked
explanation: Only a locked WORM policy guarantees data cannot be modified or deleted during the retention period, even by privileged users.

prompt: What does enabling 'Secure transfer required' on a storage account enforce?
choices: All connections must use HTTPS
A client certificate on every request
Customer-managed keys for the account
Soft delete on every container
correctAnswers: All connections must use HTTPS
explanation: Secure transfer required forces all connections onto HTTPS, rejecting plaintext HTTP. It does not demand a client certificate, which is the over-reading — transport is encrypted, whereas the caller still authenticates by key, SAS or identity as before.

prompt: What does Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) mean for Azure Storage encryption?
choices: You supply a customer-managed key from Key Vault
You manage the encryption entirely outside Azure
You share the storage account key with the clients
You disable encryption at rest for the account
correctAnswers: You supply a customer-managed key from Key Vault
explanation: BYOK means you supply a customer-managed key held in Key Vault instead of the Microsoft-managed one, so you control its rotation and revocation. Encryption at rest stays on regardless, which is the point people miss: BYOK changes who holds the key rather than whether encryption happens.

prompt: What does infrastructure (double) encryption add on top of the standard service-level encryption?
choices: A second, independent layer at the platform level
Replacement of the Microsoft keys with customer keys
Encryption applied only to the data in transit
A faster encryption algorithm for the account
correctAnswers: A second, independent layer at the platform level
explanation: Infrastructure encryption adds a second, independent layer of platform encryption for the highest-confidentiality cases. It must be chosen when the account is created and cannot be added later, which is the constraint that decides the design rather than the feature itself.

prompt: How do BYOK (customer-managed keys) and infrastructure double encryption differ?
choices: BYOK is about WHO holds the key; double is HOW MANY layers
BYOK adds a second layer; double encryption changes the owner
Both of them apply only to the data in transit
They are the same feature under two names
correctAnswers: BYOK is about WHO holds the key; double is HOW MANY layers
explanation: They are orthogonal and stack: BYOK is about who controls the key, whereas double encryption is about how many layers there are. Treating them as the same feature is the trap, since you can have either, both, or neither.

prompt: Which access-control layer does Azure Blob Storage NOT have that Azure Files (with identity-based auth) does?
choices: NTFS-style ACLs on individual files
Azure RBAC data roles on the container
Account access keys for the account
SAS tokens scoped to a single blob
correctAnswers: NTFS-style ACLs on individual files
explanation: Blob storage has no NTFS-style ACLs on individual files — that layer is what Azure Files adds on top of share-level access. RBAC data roles, SAS and account keys all exist for blob too, whereas the NTFS layer is the one genuinely missing.

prompt: A compromised admin account deletes a critical container. Which pre-configured feature would have allowed recovery within the retention window?
choices: Soft delete for containers and blobs
Infrastructure double encryption at rest
A minimum TLS version setting
Dynamic data masking on columns
correctAnswers: Soft delete for containers and blobs
explanation: Soft delete makes deleted containers/blobs recoverable during the retention window. The others don't address deletion recovery.

prompt: Why should account access keys, if used at all, be stored in Key Vault and rotated regularly?
choices: They grant full, root-like access and are high-value
Rotation is required for encryption at rest to function
Key Vault is the only place a SAS can be generated
They only work when they are stored in Key Vault
correctAnswers: They grant full, root-like access and are high-value
explanation: Account keys are root-equivalent credentials for the whole account with no built-in expiry, so vaulting and rotating them limits the damage of a leak. Better still is not using them: disabling shared-key authorization removes the credential class entirely rather than managing it.

prompt: Which recovery feature preserves the state of a blob BEFORE it is overwritten by a new upload?
choices: Blob versioning
Point-in-time restore
Immutable storage
Soft delete only
correctAnswers: Blob versioning
explanation: Versioning captures the prior version on each overwrite, which is the only one of these that preserves a state that was replaced. Soft delete is the tempting neighbour, however it recovers deletions whereas an overwrite is not a deletion — the old bytes are simply gone without versioning.

prompt: Which choice best forces all applications to use identity-based access to a storage account?
choices: Disable shared-key auth and assign RBAC data roles
Issue long-lived SAS tokens to every application involved
Enable anonymous read access for internal apps
Rotate the account access keys every day
correctAnswers: Disable shared-key auth and assign RBAC data roles
explanation: Disabling shared-key authorization is what actually forces every caller onto Entra, because RBAC roles alone leave the key path open. Rotating keys daily is the tempting hygiene answer and changes nothing structural: the key still works, just a newer one.

prompt: A user-delegation SAS is considered more secure than an account-key SAS because it is:
choices: Signed with Entra credentials, not the account key
Encrypted at rest inside an Azure Key Vault instance
Scoped to the whole subscription at once
Valid indefinitely, with no expiry at all
correctAnswers: Signed with Entra credentials, not the account key
explanation: A user-delegation SAS is signed with Entra credentials rather than the account key, so revoking it does not require rotating that key and breaking every other token. It is not indefinite — its lifetime is bounded by the delegation key, which is part of why it is the safer choice.

prompt: A storage account must encrypt data twice at the infrastructure level, using two distinct encryption algorithms so that a flaw in one does not expose the data. When can this be turned on?
choices: Only when the account is made
At any time after creation
Only on a premium account
Only with a customer-managed key
correctAnswers: Only when the account is made
explanation: Infrastructure encryption is a creation-time choice and cannot be added to an existing account, so retrofitting it means creating a new account and copying the data. Believing it can be enabled later is the costly error, because the discovery usually comes after the data has landed. It is independent of whether the key is platform-managed or customer-managed.

prompt: Which two statements about Azure Storage data-protection features are correct? (Choose two.)
choices: Soft delete undoes accidental deletion within a window
Versioning preserves the history of blob overwrites
Immutable storage can be bypassed by an owner during retention
BYOK removes the need for encryption at rest
correctAnswers: Soft delete undoes accidental deletion within a window
Versioning preserves the history of blob overwrites
explanation: Immutable storage specifically cannot be bypassed during retention, and BYOK changes key ownership, not whether encryption exists.

prompt: Which two statements about Azure Files identity-based authentication are correct? (Choose two.)
choices: Only one identity source can be enabled per storage account
Microsoft Entra Kerberos requires no on-premises domain controller
You can mix AD DS and Entra Kerberos across shares of the same account
NTFS ACLs stop applying once identity-based auth is enabled
correctAnswers: Only one identity source can be enabled per storage account
Microsoft Entra Kerberos requires no on-premises domain controller
explanation: One identity source per storage account is a hard limit, and Entra Kerberos is the domain-controller-free option. Neither distractor holds: sources cannot be mixed across shares of one account, whereas NTFS ACLs keep applying exactly as before.

prompt: Which two are ways to authorize access to a storage account? (Choose two.)
choices: Entra ID with Azure RBAC data roles
Shared access signature tokens
A network security group rule
A user-defined route on the VNet subnet
correctAnswers: Entra ID with Azure RBAC data roles
Shared access signature tokens
explanation: Entra RBAC data roles and shared access signatures both authorize access, alongside shared keys. User-defined routes and network security groups are tempting because they also gate traffic, however they control the path rather than the permission — passing an NSG is not authorization.

prompt: Referring to requirement 3 (migrate a Windows file server to Azure Files, keep NTFS permissions, no domain controller in Azure), which configuration fits?
choices: Enable Entra Kerberos and apply NTFS permissions
Enable on-premises AD DS and deploy a DC in Azure
Use Azure RBAC data roles only, without NTFS
Use SAS tokens for each user's own folder
correctAnswers: Enable Entra Kerberos and apply NTFS permissions
explanation: Entra Kerberos requires no domain controller and still supports NTFS permissions on folders, which is exactly the requirement. SAS tokens per user are the tempting alternative and would not preserve the existing folder ACLs at all.

prompt: Referring to requirement 4 (blob backups protected so even a compromised admin cannot delete or shorten retention during the retention period), which feature applies?
choices: A time-based immutable policy, Locked
Blob versioning on the container, on its own
A read-only SAS token for the container
Soft delete on its own, with nothing else
correctAnswers: A time-based immutable policy, Locked
explanation: Only a time-based immutable policy set to Locked prevents deletion and prevents the retention period being shortened, whatever privileges the attacker holds. Soft delete alone is the tempting half-measure, since it is reversible by the very administrator you are defending against.

prompt: Northwind wants the strongest, key-free way for its applications (running on Azure VMs) to read from blob storage. What should they adopt?
choices: Managed identities with RBAC data roles, shared key off
Generate long-lived account-key SAS tokens per application
Distribute the account access key to each application
Enable anonymous read access on the containers
correctAnswers: Managed identities with RBAC data roles, shared key off
explanation: Managed identities on the VMs with RBAC data roles give credential-free, identity-based access, and pairing that with disabled shared-key authorization closes the key path. Long-lived SAS tokens per application are the tempting middle ground, but they are bearer secrets that expire and need reissuing.

prompt: Order the steps to migrate an on-premises file server to Azure Files without deploying a domain controller in Azure.
reorderItems: Enable Microsoft Entra Kerberos authentication on the storage account
Assign Azure RBAC data roles for share-level access
Apply NTFS permissions on individual folders
explanation: The share and its identity source must exist before share-level RBAC can be assigned, whereas NTFS permissions come last because they sit inside the mounted share. Applying NTFS first is the ordering mistake: nothing is mounted yet, so those permissions cannot be set at all.

prompt: Order the steps to make blob backups tamper-proof for a 7-year compliance retention.
reorderItems: Enable a time-based immutability policy on the container
Set the retention period to 7 years
Confirm that deletion attempts are blocked during the retention period
explanation: The immutability policy and its retention period must be set before the policy is locked, because locking is irreversible. Locking first is the mistake that cannot be undone, whereas verification belongs last — once locked, a wrong retention period is permanent.

prompt: Configure this simplified storage account security screen to force identity-based access only, restricted to selected networks.
explanation: Disabling shared-key access forces Entra-based access, secure transfer enforces HTTPS, and selected networks closes the account to the open internet — three settings answering three different exposures. Leaving shared-key enabled is the trap here, since the other two look like a hardened account while the key path stays open.

prompt: Proposed solution: Share the storage account's primary access key with the partner. Does this solution meet the goal?
choices: Yes
No
correctAnswers: No
explanation: The account key grants broad, root-like access to the entire account with no expiry, which is the opposite of scoped and time-limited. It is tempting because it is the fastest thing to send, and that speed is exactly what makes it the wrong answer.

prompt: Proposed solution: Issue a user-delegation SAS scoped to that blob with read-only rights and an expiry. Does this solution meet the goal?
choices: Yes
No
correctAnswers: Yes
explanation: A user-delegation SAS is scoped, time-limited and revocable through Entra, whereas the account key would be none of those. Note the operational cost it accepts: the partner must be re-issued a token when it expires, which is the price of it expiring at all.

prompt: Proposed solution: Make the blob container public for anonymous read access. Does this solution meet the goal?
choices: Yes
No
correctAnswers: No
explanation: Anonymous public read exposes the blob to everyone rather than to the partner, and it carries no expiry. It is tempting because it makes the immediate problem disappear, however it fails both halves of the requirement — scoped and time-limited.

prompt: A storage account must refuse plaintext HTTP as well as any TLS version below 1.2. Fill in the two settings.
template: az storage account update --name stg1 --resource-group RG1 [[b1]] --min-tls-version [[b2]]
explanation: Two separate controls are needed and neither implies the other: HTTPS-only rejects unencrypted requests, while the minimum version rejects encrypted ones that negotiate a deprecated protocol. Note the value format, because it is not the one App Service uses: storage takes `TLS1_2`, whereas a web app takes `1.2`. Copying the working value from one service into the other is a common and confusing failure.

prompt: Complete the command that stops the storage account accepting shared-key and SAS authorization altogether, forcing every caller to authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID.
template: az storage account update --name stg1 --resource-group RG1 [[b1]] [[b2]]
explanation: Blocking shared-key access also invalidates every account-key-signed SAS, because those tokens are signed with the key being refused — which is why this switch is what makes Entra authorization mandatory rather than merely available. The three other parameters are the neighbouring toggles that get reached for instead, and each takes a different value vocabulary: `--default-action Deny` and `--public-network-access Disabled` govern network reach, whereas `--allow-blob-public-access false` governs anonymous container access.

prompt: Complete the command so that it issues a user delegation SAS for one blob — a token signed with the caller's Entra identity rather than with the account key.
template: az storage blob generate-sas --account-name stg1 --container-name docs --name file.pdf --permissions r --expiry 2026-08-01 [[b1]] [[b2]]
explanation: Both parameters are required and neither works alone: `--auth-mode login` authenticates the CLI as the signed-in principal, and `--as-user` is what makes the resulting token a user delegation SAS. `--auth-mode key` is the tempting choice because it is the default, and it produces an account-key-signed token — one that cannot be revoked without rotating the key, and that stops working the moment shared-key access is disabled.

prompt: Build the sequence that restricts a storage account to Subnet1 of VNet1 without cutting off access mid-change. Not every action in the pool belongs in the answer.
poolItems: Enable the Microsoft.Storage service endpoint on Subnet1
Add a virtual network rule on the storage account for VNet1/Subnet1
Set the storage account firewall's default action to Deny
Confirm from a VM in Subnet1 that access still works
Disable public network access on the storage account entirely
Add the office public IP range to the firewall's IP rules
Grant the Storage Blob Data Reader role to the subnet
correctOrder: Enable the Microsoft.Storage service endpoint on Subnet1
Add a virtual network rule on the storage account for VNet1/Subnet1
Set the storage account firewall's default action to Deny
Confirm from a VM in Subnet1 that access still works
explanation: A virtual network rule requires the subnet to carry the Microsoft.Storage service endpoint first, so the order is a genuine prerequisite and not a preference — and Deny comes last, because setting it before the allow rule exists cuts off every caller including yourself. The distractors are the plausible over-corrections: disabling public network access removes the endpoint the virtual network rule depends on, an office IP rule grants exactly the public access being removed, and a role cannot be assigned to a subnet because a subnet is not a security principal.

prompt: Complete the command that lets a deleted BLOB be recovered for 14 days. Container-level and versioning settings are configured separately and must not be used here.
template: az storage account blob-service-properties update --account-name stg1 --resource-group RG1 [[b1]] [[b2]]
explanation: Blob soft delete and container soft delete are two independent settings with two independent day counters, and enabling the container one does not protect a blob deleted inside a container that still exists. Versioning keeps previous versions of a blob that is overwritten rather than recovering one that is deleted, and a restore policy is point-in-time restore, which depends on versioning and change feed instead of standing alone.

prompt: A storage account holds containers, blobs, queues, and tables. An application must be given a credential that reaches the data in one specified table and nothing else in the account. Which authentication method should you use?
choices: A service SAS token
A user delegation SAS
An account SAS token
A shared account key
correctAnswers: A service SAS token
explanation: A service SAS is the only form that can be scoped to a single table. A user delegation SAS is the tempting answer because it is the most modern and Entra-backed option, but it is available for Blob storage only, so it cannot address a table at all. An account SAS and a shared key both reach the whole account, which is exactly what must be avoided.

prompt: An application shares more than 1,000 files from Blob storage with external users who do not authenticate with Microsoft Entra. Access to each file must be restricted to one IP address, different for each file. What should you do?
choices: Generate a service SAS with signedIP
Configure the storage account firewall
Set Require secure transfer on the account
Enable anonymous public read access
correctAnswers: Generate a service SAS with signedIP
explanation: The `signedIP` field pins an individual SAS to one address, and a separate SAS can be issued per file, so the design scales past a thousand files. The account firewall is the tempting answer because it also filters by IP, but it caps out well below a thousand rules and applies to the account rather than per file. Requiring secure transfer blocks HTTP without restricting where a request comes from.

prompt: An application authenticates with Microsoft Entra and must read blobs in one container of a storage account, and nothing else in that account. The solution must follow the principle of least privilege. What should you assign to its managed identity?
choices: Storage Blob Data Reader
Storage Blob Data Contributor
Storage Account Contributor
The account access key
correctAnswers: Storage Blob Data Reader
explanation: Storage Blob Data Reader is a data-plane role that can be assigned at container scope, so the application reads that container and reaches nothing else. Storage Blob Data Contributor is the trap because it would also work, adding write and delete the application never needs. Storage Account Contributor manages the account without granting data access at all, and an access key reaches every service in the account.

prompt: Blobs deleted by mistake must be recoverable for 30 days. Keeping a copy of every intermediate write is not required. The solution must minimize cost. What should you enable?
choices: Blob soft delete on it
Blob versioning on the account
An immutability policy on it
A backup vault for the blobs
correctAnswers: Blob soft delete on it
explanation: Soft delete retains only what was deleted, for the window you set, so it costs the least of the options that meet the requirement. Versioning is the trap: it recovers a deleted blob just as well, but it also stores every intermediate version, which the scenario says is not needed and which is what makes it dearer. An immutability policy prevents deletion outright rather than allowing recovery.

prompt: Audit logs in a storage account must survive the loss of an entire Azure region. Read access to the secondary region during normal operation is not required. The solution must minimize cost. Which redundancy option should you choose?
choices: Geo-redundant storage (GRS)
Read-access GRS (RA-GRS)
Zone-redundant storage (ZRS)
Locally redundant storage (LRS)
correctAnswers: Geo-redundant storage (GRS)
explanation: GRS replicates to a paired region, which is what surviving a regional loss requires, and it is the cheapest option that does so. RA-GRS is the trap because it offers the same durability and looks strictly better, but the read endpoint it adds is billed and the scenario says it is not needed. ZRS survives a zone rather than a region, and LRS survives neither.
